summary: Nebuchadnezzar is troubled by dreams and demands that Babylon's experts tell both the dream and its interpretation. When the demand becomes a death sentence for the wise men, Daniel asks his companions to seek mercy from the God of heaven, receives the secret in a night vision, and tells the king of a great image shattered by a stone. The chapter ends with Nebuchadnezzar acknowledging Daniel's God as a revealer of secrets and promoting Daniel and his companions.
whyItMatters: This chapter introduces a central Daniel pattern: imperial power makes impossible demands, while God gives wisdom that the court cannot supply. It also sets up the book's long view of kingdoms as temporary before a kingdom God establishes.

context.author: The book contains third-person court stories about Daniel and first-person visions later in the book. Traditional readers identify Daniel as author; many critical scholars understand the final form as anonymous, using older Daniel traditions.
context.audience: Jews under pressure to surrender worship, practice, identity, or hope under imperial power.
context.date: The stories are set in the sixth-century BC Babylonian exile and Persian period. Many scholars date the final Hebrew-Aramaic form to about 167-164 BC, while traditional readings place authorship in Daniel's sixth-century setting.
context.setting: This chapter is set in Nebuchadnezzar's Babylonian court after Judah's elite have been deported. Daniel and his companions are Judean exiles serving inside that court.
context.literaryForm: Court tale within Daniel's bilingual Hebrew-Aramaic book; at 2:4 the text signals a move into the Aramaic section that continues through chapter 7.

outline.heading: The king's impossible demand
outline.note: Nebuchadnezzar is troubled by a dream, demands both the dream and its interpretation, rejects the experts' plea, and orders the wise men killed.

outline.heading: Daniel seeks mercy
outline.note: Daniel responds with counsel and prudence, asks for time, and tells Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah to seek mercies from the God of heaven.

outline.heading: The secret is revealed
outline.note: The secret is revealed to Daniel in a night vision, and Daniel blesses God for wisdom, power, and disclosure.

outline.heading: Daniel before the king
outline.note: Daniel stops the destruction of the wise men and tells Nebuchadnezzar that no court expert can reveal the secret, but God in heaven can.

outline.heading: The dream described
outline.note: Daniel describes the great image made of metals and clay, then a stone that breaks it and becomes a mountain filling the whole earth.

outline.heading: The dream interpreted
outline.note: Daniel identifies Nebuchadnezzar as the head of gold, describes later kingdoms, and says God will set up a kingdom that will never be destroyed.

outline.heading: The king responds
outline.note: Nebuchadnezzar honors Daniel, acknowledges Daniel's God as revealer of secrets, and promotes Daniel and his companions.

keyVerses.text: that they would desire mercies of the God of heaven concerning this secret, that Daniel and his companions would not perish with the rest of the wise men of Babylon.
keyVerses.why: This verse shows Daniel's first response to the crisis: he gathers his companions to seek mercy rather than claiming personal control.

keyVerses.text: He reveals the deep and secret things. He knows what is in the darkness, and the light dwells with him.
keyVerses.why: Daniel's praise names the chapter's central contrast between hidden royal mysteries and God's knowledge.

keyVerses.text: but there is a God in heaven who reveals secrets, and he has made known to King Nebuchadnezzar what will be in the latter days. Your dream and the visions of your head on your bed are these:
keyVerses.why: Daniel states plainly that the interpretation comes from God, not from ordinary court wisdom.

keyVerses.text: “In the days of those kings the God of heaven will set up a kingdom which will never be destroyed, nor will its sovereignty be left to another people; but it will break in pieces and consume all these kingdoms, and it will stand forever.
keyVerses.why: This is the climax of the interpretation: the kingdoms in the image are temporary, but God's kingdom is described as enduring.

questions.question: Why does Nebuchadnezzar demand both the dream and the interpretation?
questions.answer: The chapter says his spirit was troubled and that he wanted the experts to make known both the dream and its interpretation. He treats their inability to tell the dream as proof that their interpretation cannot be trusted. The text does not explain whether he forgot the dream or was testing them, so readers should not press beyond the scene's stated demand.

questions.question: Who are the Chaldeans in this chapter?
questions.answer: They are part of the group summoned with magicians, enchanters, and sorcerers to tell the king his dreams. In the scene, they speak for the court experts and say no human can meet the king's demand. The chapter uses them as representatives of Babylonian expertise, without giving a detailed job description.

questions.question: Why are Daniel and his companions in danger if they did not appear before the king at first?
questions.answer: The decree targets all the wise men of Babylon. Verse 13 says the wise men were to be slain and that Daniel and his companions were sought to be slain. The chapter assumes they belong to the affected court category, even though Daniel enters the scene after the first confrontation.

questions.question: What does Daniel do before giving an answer?
questions.answer: Daniel first speaks to Arioch with counsel and prudence, asks the king for time, and tells his companions about the danger. Then they seek mercies from the God of heaven concerning the secret. The order matters in the story: Daniel acts carefully, but the answer comes by revelation.

questions.question: Does Daniel claim the dream was revealed because he is wiser than everyone else?
questions.answer: No. Daniel tells the king that the secret was not revealed to him because he has more wisdom than any living person. He says the purpose is that the interpretation may be made known to the king and that the king may know the thoughts of his heart.

questions.question: What is the great image made of?
questions.answer: The image has a head of fine gold, chest and arms of silver, belly and thighs of bronze, legs of iron, and feet partly of iron and partly of clay. Daniel later explains the head of gold as Nebuchadnezzar and describes successive kingdoms after him. Readers differ over the exact historical identification of the later kingdoms, which the chapter does not name.

questions.question: What does the stone do in the dream?
questions.answer: The stone is cut out without hands, strikes the image on its feet, and breaks the metals and clay in pieces. Daniel interprets this as God's kingdom breaking and consuming the other kingdoms and standing forever. Later Jewish and Christian readers connect this image in different ways to hope for God's rule; the chapter itself explains the stone in terms of a kingdom God sets up.

questions.question: Why does Nebuchadnezzar worship Daniel, and is the chapter endorsing that?
questions.answer: Verse 46 says Nebuchadnezzar fell on his face, worshiped Daniel, and ordered offerings and sweet odors for him. The next verse records the king's confession that Daniel's God is the God of gods, Lord of kings, and revealer of secrets. The narrative reports the king's response, but it does not pause to explain whether every part of that response is proper.

questions.question: What changes for Daniel and his companions at the end?
questions.answer: The king gives Daniel gifts, makes him ruler over the province of Babylon, and makes him chief governor over the wise men. Daniel then requests positions for Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego over the affairs of the province, while Daniel remains in the king's gate. The chapter closes with endangered exiles now holding authority inside the same empire that threatened them.

glossary.def: Court experts summoned with magicians, enchanters, and sorcerers to address the king's dream; in this chapter they cannot provide the dream or its interpretation.
The hidden matter of the dream and its meaning, which Daniel says God reveals.
Daniel's title for God when asking mercy, praising the revelation, and explaining who gives and removes royal power.
The group threatened by Nebuchadnezzar's decree and later spared when Daniel reveals the interpretation.
